current_episode.title: 452: The Words That Quietly Give Away Your Power

guest.bio_context: Kim Porter holds an engineering science and mechanics degree with an emphasis in biomedical engineering from Iowa State University, earned in the early 1980s before biomedical engineering was an established field. She began her career working on next-generation spacesuit gloves following the Challenger disaster in 1986, then moved to product design at Nike, and spent nearly her entire 40-year career as the only woman in all-male engineering environments. She founded HatchOne, an online engineering community that includes a Women in Engineering subgroup, and has recently retired from full-time work while continuing to run the community and her consultancy.

pending_qa.q: What language changes does Kim Porter recommend engineers use to avoid undermining their own authority?
pending_qa.r: Kim Porter advises eliminating phrases like 'I think' and 'I believe' from professional vocabulary entirely, calling them self-undermining. Instead, she recommends leading with 'Here is the data, these are the results, I recommend we do this' — a framing she summarizes as 'no opinions, all data, no emotion.' She says this removes subjectivity and leaves no opinion to argue against, only data.

pending_qa.q: How did Kim Porter get her first engineering job and what surprised her about it?
pending_qa.r: After reading a job ad in the New York Times for a biomechanics engineer, Kim Porter applied to a company that held the contract to manufacture and design the shuttle spacesuit, joining the project in 1986 immediately after the Challenger accident to work on next-generation spacesuit gloves and biomechanical analysis. She was surprised to discover she had no passion for aerospace as a market channel, despite finding the job itself excellent, and pivoted to Nike as soon as the opportunity arose.

pending_qa.q: What is Kim Porter's advice for early-career engineers choosing their first job?
pending_qa.r: Kim Porter warns that entry-level engineers who take a first job without researching whether it aligns with their interests risk being pigeonholed — for example, a mechanical engineer who wants consumer electronics but spends two or three years at an automobile company will find it very difficult to pivot. She advises identifying your desired industry early and using an exercise of writing three to five short stories about moments of childhood bliss between ages 6 and 10, then analyzing the action verbs to identify your true professional purpose.

pending_qa.q: How does Kim Porter recommend women engineers respond when told they are 'too assertive' or 'too aggressive' in performance reviews?
pending_qa.r: Kim Porter says early in her career she would apologize and promise to do better, but later she pushed back directly with facts — pointing out, for example, that a male colleague who yells in meetings is not labeled aggressive. She advises having proof of respectful, data-driven conduct with integrity so there is nothing more to be said, and recounts telling bosses and VPs directly: 'You can fire me before I will do that.'

pending_qa.q: What is Kim Porter's 'silence is power' communication strategy in professional settings?
pending_qa.r: Kim Porter coaches that once you have presented a data-driven recommendation, you should stop talking completely and let silence sit. She explains that people are uncomfortable with silence and will naturally fill the void, which shifts conversational power to the presenter. She frames this as a leadership power move that works because when there is only data and no opinion on the table, there is nothing subjective to argue against.

pending_qa.q: What does Kim Porter say distinguishes a true leader from a manager in engineering environments?
pending_qa.r: Kim Porter argues that engineers are trained to be precise, accurate, and perfect — traits that must be partially unlearned to become an effective leader. She says a true leader openly owns their mistakes and creates psychological safety for their team to fail without consequences, whereas a manager who micromanages, hides errors, and takes credit for others' work is not a leader but someone who does not think well enough of themselves to lead authentically.

pending_qa.q: Why does Kim Porter believe new engineering disciplines like biomedical and environmental engineering have better gender representation than mechanical engineering?
pending_qa.r: Kim Porter, drawing on a discussion held in her Women in Engineering group where a participant queried ChatGPT on the topic, explains that newer disciplines like biomedical and environmental engineering do not carry the 50-year legacy of institutional misogyny that older fields like mechanical engineering do. Mechanical engineering still sits at roughly one woman for every nine men — the same ratio as when she was a student — while biomedical engineering is now approximately 50-50 and environmental engineering is around 30 to 40 percent women.

pending_qa.q: How did Kim Porter build HatchOne and use TikTok to grow an engineering community?
pending_qa.r: About a year before the interview, Kim Porter was sitting on her couch feeling bored in retirement and decided to study the TikTok algorithm, which she believes is far more powerful than most people recognize. She used TikTok as a funnel to build HatchOne, an online engineering community that includes a Women in Engineering subgroup, and describes the experience as fulfilling and something she is having a blast running.
